items.stimulus: Folklorists have long assumed that riddles passed down by word of mouth change quickly as they move from one teller to the next. To test this, researcher Amara Okafor recorded the same twelve riddles from grandparents and their grandchildren in three Ghanaian villages. More than 80 percent of the riddles were worded almost identically across the two generations. Oral riddles, her findings suggest, can be far more stable than scholars had believed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a study whose results challenge a common assumption about how oral riddles change over time
To describe a study that was unable to determine whether oral riddles change from one generation to the next
To compare the riddles told in three Ghanaian villages with riddles collected in other parts of the world
To explain why grandchildren prefer to repeat riddles in exactly the words their grandparents once used
items.explanation: The text opens with an old belief (riddles change quickly), then describes Okafor's recordings and ends with a clear result: the riddles stayed nearly identical. So the text describes a study, and that study's findings challenge the assumption. Choice A names both parts.

B.why: You saw 'describe a study' and stopped reading. The text gives a clear result: over 80 percent of the riddles matched. The question was answered, not left open.

C.why: You picked a comparison, but the text never mentions riddles from anywhere else. It only reports what Okafor found in the three villages.

D.why: You read a motive into the findings. The study shows that the wording stayed the same. It says nothing about what the grandchildren prefer or why they repeat the riddles that way.

items.stimulus: An earthquake sends out two main kinds of waves. Primary waves are fast but usually cause little damage, while secondary waves travel more slowly and do most of the shaking. Earthquake early-warning systems take advantage of this gap. Sensors near the fault detect the primary waves, computers estimate the quake's location and strength within seconds, and alerts go out to phones before the secondary waves arrive.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how early-warning systems use the difference between two waves to alert people before strong shaking
To describe the method that computers use to estimate an earthquake's location from the data that sensors collect
To compare primary and secondary waves in order to show which kind is more dangerous to buildings and people
To argue that earthquake early-warning systems are too slow to give people any useful notice before shaking
items.explanation: The text sets up a fact (fast, weak waves and slow, damaging waves) and then walks through each step of a warning system that uses that gap: detect, estimate, alert. Choice A names the whole mechanism.

B.why: You took one step of the process for the whole thing. Estimating the quake's location is only the middle step. The text is about how the full system turns the gap between the waves into a warning.

C.why: This is the comparison trap. The text does contrast the two waves, but only as setup. Its main job is explaining the warning system, not ranking which wave is more dangerous.

D.why: You read an evaluation into a text that only explains. The text says the alerts arrive before the secondary waves, which is the opposite of 'too slow.'

items.stimulus: Sea cucumbers are often treated as passive scavengers that simply drift across the seafloor eating debris. Marine biologist Lena Varga, however, placed sea cucumbers in tanks of reef sediment and measured the sediment's chemistry over six weeks. Sediment that the animals had digested contained more dissolved nutrients and was less acidic than untouched sediment, changes that can help nearby corals grow.

To describe research showing that sea cucumbers have little measurable effect on the sediment they digest
To explain how sea cucumbers move across the seafloor while searching for debris to eat
To argue that coral reefs cannot survive in any location where sea cucumbers are absent

items.stimulus: Before satellites, mapmakers charted entire countries using a method called triangulation. Surveyors first measured a single straight baseline on the ground with great care. From each end of that line, they sighted a distant landmark and recorded the angles. Because a triangle's unknown sides can be calculated from one side and two angles, each new triangle supplied a baseline for the next, extending the survey across hundreds of miles.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how triangulation let surveyors map large regions starting from one carefully measured line
To describe how surveyors decided which distant landmarks were most suitable for recording angles
To compare the accuracy of triangulation surveys with the accuracy of modern satellite mapping
To argue that triangulation produced maps too inaccurate to be useful across very large distances
items.explanation: The text walks through a process step by step: measure a baseline, sight landmarks, calculate the sides, and chain the triangles together. Choice A names the whole mechanism and what it achieved.

B.why: You chose one step instead of the whole process. The text mentions sighting landmarks but never explains how surveyors chose them.

C.why: This is the comparison trap. Satellites appear only as a time marker in the first sentence. The text explains one method and never compares accuracy.

D.why: You assumed the text evaluates the method. It only explains it, and it says triangulation extended surveys 'across hundreds of miles', which is the opposite of 'too inaccurate.'

items.stimulus: Many athletes sit in cold water after hard workouts because they believe it speeds recovery. To test this belief, researchers had 24 runners complete an intense track session. Half of the runners then sat in 10°C water for ten minutes, and the other half rested on a bench. The next day, every runner ran a timed 200-meter sprint. The two groups' times were nearly identical, which suggests that the cold soak gave no advantage in next-day speed.
items.stem: What is this text mainly doing?
choices: Describing a study that found cold-water soaks did not make runners faster the next day
Arguing that the researchers used too few runners to support any conclusion at all
Describing a study that left unclear whether cold-water soaks affect next-day speed
Explaining how cold water changes runners' muscle tissue after a hard workout
items.explanation: The text sets up a belief, describes a test (cold soak or rest), and ends with a clear result: the sprint times were nearly identical. It only reports. items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: When clover grows in a field, soil bacteria called rhizobia enter its roots and form small swellings known as nodules. Inside these nodules, the bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form that plants can absorb. In return, the clover feeds the bacteria sugars it makes through photosynthesis. When the clover later dies and decays, the nitrogen stored in its tissues is released into the soil, where the next crop planted in that field can take it up.
items.stem: What is this text mainly doing?
choices: Comparing how clover and other crops each take up nitrogen from the soil
Arguing that farmers should plant clover instead of buying chemical fertilizer
Explaining how clover, with the help of bacteria, adds usable nitrogen to soil
Explaining how clover removes nitrogen from soil, leaving less for later crops
items.explanation: This is a process text. Bacteria enter the roots, form nodules, and turn air nitrogen into a usable form. The clover feeds them, and when it decays the nitrogen goes into the soil for the next crop. The right choice names the whole mechanism from start to finish. On the real 'main purpose' question, a process passage almost always calls for an 'explain how' answer that covers every step, not just one of them.

A.why: This is the classic trap for process texts. The choice claims a comparison, but the text explains only one plant. 'The next crop' is mentioned only as the receiver of the nitrogen, never as something being compared.

B.why: You turned an explanation into a recommendation. The text never mentions fertilizer and never tells farmers what to do. It only describes how the process works.

D.why: You flipped the direction of the process. The text says clover adds nitrogen to the soil when it decays, so later crops get more nitrogen, not less.

items.stimulus: Most earthquakes release built-up stress within seconds. Along some subduction zones, however, the boundary between two plates can slip over weeks without producing strong shaking. In these slow slip events, fluids squeezed out of the descending plate collect along the fault and reduce the friction that normally locks the plates together. The plates then creep past each other a few centimeters at a time, and that movement can transfer stress to neighboring, still-locked segments of the fault, which may later rupture in ordinary earthquakes.

choices: To explain how slow slip events occur and how they can affect nearby segments of a fault
To compare how often slow slip events and ordinary earthquakes occur along subduction zones

items.stimulus: Because trees in warm climates tend to have smooth-edged leaves, paleobotanists have long estimated ancient temperatures from the share of smooth-edged species in a fossil flora. items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: The blank interiors on many eighteenth-century maps of Africa are often read as simple ignorance: mapmakers drew what they knew and left the rest empty. Historian Lena Marchetti, however, compared the printed maps of one Parisian workshop with its surviving notebooks. The notebooks record rivers, towns, and mountain ranges in those 'empty' regions, drawn from travelers' reports. Only features described by at least two independent travelers ever reached the printed maps.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe research suggesting that some blank areas on old maps reflected a standard for confirming reports rather than a lack of reports.
To describe research suggesting that some blank areas on old maps were left empty to keep geographic knowledge from rival powers.
To describe research confirming that blank areas on old maps marked regions about which mapmakers had received no reports.
To explain how one Parisian workshop gathered and recorded travelers' accounts of distant rivers, towns, and mountains.
items.explanation: The common view says the blanks mean the mapmakers had no information. The notebooks show the workshop did have reports about those regions. The last sentence explains why the reports were left off: a feature reached the printed map only if two independent travelers described it. So the blanks reflect a rule for confirming reports, which is what A says.

B.why: You correctly saw that the omissions were deliberate, then supplied a motive the text never gives. The only reason it offers is the two-traveler rule, not secrecy.

C.why: This is the old view that the text rejects after 'however.' The notebooks show the mapmakers did have reports about the blank regions.

D.why: The notebooks are the evidence, not the subject. The text uses them to reinterpret the blank areas, not to describe how the workshop collected information.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Because trees in cold climates tend to have toothed leaves and those in warm climates smooth-edged ones, paleobotanists estimate past temperatures from the share of toothed leaves among fossils. Most such fossils, though, were buried in ancient streambeds. Ana Lindqvist sampled leaves settling in modern streambeds and compared them with leaves from the surrounding forests. Toothed leaves were overrepresented in the streams, because streamside trees, which tend to be toothed regardless of climate, shed directly into the water. Temperatures calculated from the stream samples came out several degrees colder than those calculated from the forests.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a study indicating that past temperatures estimated from fossil leaves buried in stream deposits may be too cold.
To describe a study indicating that a leaf's edge reveals little about the climate in which the tree that grew it lived.
To describe a study indicating that ancient streambeds held fewer toothed leaves than the forests around them did.
To explain why trees that grow beside streams tend to produce toothed leaves no matter what the climate is.
items.explanation: This takes three steps. First, the method depends on what share of fossil leaves are toothed. Second, most fossils come from streambeds. Third, the modern streambed samples contained too many toothed leaves and gave colder temperatures. Put together, the study points to a cold bias in estimates from stream deposits, which is A.

B.why: You saw that the study criticizes the method and stretched that into rejecting the method's basis. The study only finds a bias in where the samples come from. The general link between leaf edges and climate is left standing.

C.why: This reverses the finding, since stream samples had more toothed leaves, not fewer. It also swaps the modern streambeds that were sampled for ancient ones.

D.why: The text says streamside trees tend to be toothed regardless of climate but never explains why. That detail is one link in the argument, not its purpose.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Cold-water fish in summer often gather at the downstream ends of gravel bars, and for years this was credited to hidden springs. Hydrologists now trace the cooling to the river itself. Where a riffle steepens, the current forces some river water down into the gravel. Moving slowly through the bed, that water gives up heat to sediment kept cool by the night and by the ground beneath. It then wells back into the channel at the bar's lower end, several degrees colder than the flow around it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how river water passing through a gravel bar is cooled and then returned to the channel as a cold pocket.
To explain how springs beneath gravel bars supply the cold water that collects at the bars' downstream ends.
To explain how a steepening riffle forces part of a river's current down into the gravel beneath it.
To compare the temperatures cold-water fish prefer with the temperatures of a river's water in summer.
items.explanation: After setting aside the old explanation, the text follows one mechanism from start to finish. River water is pushed into the gravel, cools as it moves slowly through the bed, and comes back out colder at the bar's lower end. A names the whole cycle and its result.

B.why: This is the old belief the text replaces. The second sentence credits the cooling to the river itself, not to springs.

C.why: You picked a true step and treated it as the whole process. Going down into the gravel is only the first stage. The cooling and the return are the point.

D.why: The fish only introduce the puzzle. The text gives no preferred temperatures and makes no comparison, because it explains a single mechanism.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Thunderstorms form more often downwind of large cities than upwind, and the usual explanation is heat: pavement warms the air, which rises and builds clouds. Meteorologist Priya Natarajan set out to test this with a weather model of Atlanta. Removing the city's extra heat from the model barely changed how many storms formed downwind. Removing its buildings, however, cut those storms by nearly half; the tall structures had been slowing incoming winds, forcing air to pile up and rise.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a modeling study suggesting that a city's buildings, more than its heat, account for the extra storms downwind.
To describe a modeling study supporting the view that heat from a city's pavement accounts for the extra storms downwind.
To describe a modeling study that ruled out heat as the source of the extra storms downwind without finding another source.
To compare how often thunderstorms form near Atlanta with how often they form near other large cities.
items.explanation: The study tests the usual heat explanation and finds that removing the heat barely mattered. It then finds that removing the buildings cut the downwind storms nearly in half, and it says how: the buildings slowed the wind and forced air upward. A names both results, heat set aside and buildings identified as the cause.

B.why: You read the first sentence's explanation as the text's conclusion. The model showed that removing the heat 'barely changed' how many storms formed, so the study undercuts this view.

C.why: You correctly saw that heat was set aside but stopped before the 'however' sentence. The study names another cause, buildings slowing the wind, and explains how it works.

D.why: Only Atlanta is modeled, and the comparison in the text is between versions of the model with and without heat or buildings, not between cities.
